newsitem.title: USA: Potential juror quizzes Oklahoma bomb prosecutors.
newsitem.headline: Potential juror quizzes Oklahoma bomb prosecutors.

text.p: A potential juror in the Oklahoma City bombing case turned the tables on prosecutors on Tuesday, asking them for details of bomb scene evidence.

The rancher and pilot, who said he was an explosives expert, was the 40th prospective juror questioned by the judge and attorneys as they select a jury to decide the fate of accused bomber Timothy McVeigh.
He also told the court he owned a gun barrel firm in Mexico and in the 1970s flew internationally for the U.S. government.

Out of the blue, the man began expounding on his unanswered questions about the bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building in 1995 that killed 168 people. He said he suspected the bomb was detonated electronically.

He also said the thumbnail was normally used to strip coating off the wire used to detonate a bomb, prompting him to wonder if authorities had carried out any DNA testing on the bomb debris at the site.
"That's a question driving me nuts," he said.
"I wish I could help," Patrick Ryan, U.S. Attorney for Oklahoma City, told the man, without answering his question.
Ryan began to treat the man almost like an expert witness, asking him about the velocity of detonation of an ammonium nitrate fuel oil bomb. The man said "between 8,000 and 11,000 feet per second."
The government has said the bomb used to blow up the Murrah building was made of ammonium nitrate, fuel and other explosives.

The man who also said he was shot twice during an attempted hijacking of his plane in the U.S. Virgin Islands refused to say whether he had U.S. security clearance when he worked for the government. He also said he did not know if he had ever killed anyone.
Federal Judge Richard Matsch asked the man if he would "be his own expert" if there were disagreements between expert witnesses called in the trial, and he agreed it could be a problem.
McVeigh's attorneys did not question the man.
Earlier in the session, Matsch excused a potential juror from serving, saying he did not believe she could be impartial.

The woman, a German-born naturalised U.S. citizen in her late 50s, had written in a questionnaire that she disagreed with Matsch's decision to move the trial from Oklahoma to Denver to ensure McVeigh a fair hearing.

The three-times divorced woman, who said she was physically abused by two husbands, suffered from high blood pressure and feared the stress of a high-profile trial might affect her health. She was the second person publicly and immediately excused since jury selection began last week.
One woman was dismissed last week because she had been treated for stress and feared breaking down.
The identity of the potential jurors is kept secret and they sit behind a wooden panel in the courtroom.
